faq_slots.question: Why has a tile come loose, and will the others follow?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Three genuinely different causes in plain words: adhesive that never gripped the whole back of the tile (dabs, not a solid bed, or a dusty or painted wall), a floor or wall that moves under it (floorboards that flex, no gap left for movement), and water that got behind and softened what the tile was stuck to. Then what the local housing adds, then the fix: the cause first, the tile second.

faq_slots.question: Porcelain or ceramic: which is better for a floor?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the Table E porcelain and ceramic row: porcelain is a ceramic tile that takes in very little water, which suits floors, wet rooms and outside, but the right tile depends on where it goes and what it has to put up with (wear, slip where it gets wet, frost outside), not on the name. Never a rating as proof (the Table E slip row), never that porcelain is always better.

faq_slots.question: Does new plaster or a new floor need to dry before it's tiled?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Yes: from the Table E new plaster and concrete row, new plaster and a new screed are left to dry and checked before a tile goes on, the waits as the row gives them and no other figure; a heated screed is run up and cooled before tiling (the Table E UFH row). Say why: tiles fixed over a wet base let go or crack as it dries out. No dates.

faq_slots.question: Do I need permission for tiling work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": tiling at a home usually needs no permission; a listed home where the floor or wall is part of what is listed usually needs consent before it is altered; a hard surface at the front of the house usually needs the rain to soak away inside the garden; electrical work for a heated floor in a bathroom is notified through the electrician, never the tiler; a drain moved in a wet room goes through building control. cards.title: A bathroom, kitchen or floor you're redoing
cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: the household is refitting a bathroom, a kitchen or a hall floor, the old tiles or the paint are still up, and the tiles are chosen or nearly. What decides it: what is behind or under them (plaster, plasterboard, cement board, a screed, floorboards on joists) and whether it can carry the weight of the tiles they want (the Table E plaster and plasterboard row, with no figure), whether a shower or bath edge needs a waterproof layer first, and whether anything new, plaster or a screed, still has to dry out (the Table E new plaster and concrete row, the wait as the row gives it). What the work gives them, in plain words: the right board or layer put on first, the tiles fixed so they stay put, silicone where the surfaces meet. On a page whose services are mostly repairs the card reads as the room they are patching up and whether it is worth tiling again from the wall out. Never a lifestyle pitch, never the finish sold on its own, never a fault invented for a new room.
cards.mechanism: whether the wall or floor is ready to carry tiles

cards.title: Water getting behind the tiles
cards.brief: Problem led: grout missing or dark in one corner of the shower however often it is cleaned, a wall that feels damp, a tile near the bath that has gone loose, a mark on the ceiling of the room below (the Table B bathroom and wet room signs). The one cause this card makes: there is nothing waterproof under the tiles, so what gets through the grout reaches the board or plaster behind, which softens and lets go (the Table E rows: tiles are not tanking; plasterboard in a shower). Say what putting it right usually involves from the Table A bathroom and wet room stages: the tiles off in the wet area, soft board replaced, a tanking layer over it and its corners, then the tiles, with silicone and not grout where the wall meets the bath, the tray or the floor. New grout over the old joints is not the fix, and the card says so without alarm. Never 'waterproof grout', never a system or membrane name unless [CV: materials_methods] gives it, never that this business tanks every job unless confirmed. Not a joint that was sealed rigid: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: nothing waterproof beneath the tiles in a wet area

cards.title: Cracks that run from one tile to the next
cards.brief: Problem led: a crack through several tiles in a row, grout breaking up along one line, tiles that rock or sound hollow, a floor that feels uneven (the Table B floor tiling signs). The one cause this card makes: the floor is moving and the tiles were fixed rigid to it, so the movement comes through them: floorboards that flex, a crack or joint in the screed below, no gap left at the edges or across a large floor. Say what the fix usually involves from the Table A floor stages and the Table E movement joint rows: the floor checked for flatness and give before anything goes down, stiffened or overlaid where it flexes, a decoupling layer as one option on a timber floor, joints left where the floor needs them and filled with something that gives. Swapping only the cracked tiles sets fresh tiles on top of the same moving floor. Never a joint spacing or width figure (the rows carry them). On a page with period floors the card also reads as loose and missing pieces over a base that has shifted or gone damp; with outdoor tiling, slabs that have lifted after a winter on a base that moved.
cards.mechanism: a floor that moves under tiles fixed rigid to it

cards.title: One broken tile, and whether a swap will hold
cards.brief: The repair customer's situation and the honest answer to it: a floor tile cracked by something dropped, a chipped edge, a tile fallen off the splashback, grout splitting round one tile (the Table B repairs signs). What decides it: whether the knock did it, in which case one tile out and a matching one in is a fair repair (the Table A repair stages: the neighbours checked, the tile removed without harming the ones round it), or whether the cause sits behind or under it, water, movement or adhesive in dabs, in which case a new tile goes the same way (the Table B repairs row: a replacement fails if the cause is not put right). What the work gives them: a straight answer on which it is before anything is ordered, and a matching spare where one exists, never promised. Never a scare, never a dig at whoever laid it, never that every crack is a floor problem: card 3 owns the line of cracks.
cards.mechanism: whether the knock or what sits under the tile did the damage

cards.title: What it will need from you afterwards
cards.brief: The customer's situation: they want to know what they are taking on once the job is done. What decides it: what the tiles, the grout and the seals need, from the Table A and E rows for this service: grout lets a little water through and dries out between uses, so a shower is aired and the corners watched; silicone is renewed when it comes away rather than grouted over; some stones are resealed on a timetable that depends on the stone, the product and the use (never an interval: the Table E stone sealing row) and are never cleaned with anything acidic; a heated floor is brought up to temperature gradually; outside, the joints and the drainage are kept clear so water does not sit and freeze. What the work gives them: an honest picture of what it saves them and what it does not. Never a promise about how it will look or last; a return visit or aftercare only where the services list or the confirmed practices (aftercare_advice) have it.
cards.mechanism: what the tiles, the grout and the seals need through the years

cards.title: Floors that flex in the older streets
cards.brief: Tiles that crack along a line, grout that breaks up, a hall floor that bounces. The one cause this card makes: timber floors on joists and lime plaster, from the era the town's older streets were built in, which the town profile dates; 'were built with', never 'have', and never the state of anyone's bathroom today. Tie the era to what it means for the work and nothing else: a timber floor stiffened or overlaid before tiles go down, an adhesive chosen for a floor that moves, a decoupling layer as one option, and a lime plastered wall checked for the weight it can carry (the Table A floor stages and the Table E rows, with no figure). Not a floor that moves under rigid tiles as the cause: the category page owns that; here the cause is how the era built.
cards.mechanism: timber floors on joists from the era the older streets were built in

cards.title: Period hallways with pieces missing
cards.brief: Loose or missing pieces in a geometric hall floor, white salts that keep coming back, a hall that feels damp underfoot (the Table B period floor signs). The one cause this card makes: a floor laid straight on the ground in the era the town profile gives, with damp and salts moving up through it; an era claim (built with such floors), never that the hallways are in a state. What it means for the work, from the Table A and E period floor rows: sound pieces kept, lifting only where there is a reason, compatible replacements and a bedding that suits the original, and no sealer that traps the damp in. Where the home is listed, consent before the floor is altered, as 'usually' and never the Act's name. Not a tile cracked by a knock: the repair pages own that.
cards.mechanism: damp and salts moving up through a floor laid on the ground

cards.title: New estates settling in their first years
cards.brief: Hairline cracks in grout, a tile gone hollow in a bathroom a few years old, a floor tile that rocks. The one cause this card makes: the plasterboard walls and chipboard floors the newer estates were built with, which dry out and settle after the build (the town profile gives the estates). What it means for the work: the weight a plasterboard wall can carry before it needs a board over it (the Table E plaster and plasterboard row, no figure), a chipboard floor overlaid or decoupled before tiles, joints left where the floor needs them. Never a judgement on the builder or the homes. Not adhesive in dabs: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: plasterboard walls and chipboard floors drying out and settling after the build

cards.title: Hard water marking the grout
cards.brief: Grout lines that go pale and rough, a shower screen that will not come clean, dark corners that come back. Only where the town profile gives the water hardness from the supplier's data; otherwise the card reads as flats and their leases (some leases restrict hard floors or ask for a sound deadening layer under them, from the profile only). The one cause this card makes: limescale from the water settling into grout that lets water through, and on glass. What it means for the work: the grout chosen with that in mind (a resin grout as one option from the Table A regrouting cell, never a brand), silicone kept sound, and the aftercare that goes with it. Never a hardness figure the research does not give.
cards.mechanism: limescale from the town's water settling into porous grout and on glass

cards.title: Flats, stairs and the lease
cards.brief: Where the town profile gives a high share of flats: tiles, boards and bagged adhesive carried up by hand, a skip that has to sit on the road (the skip firm's permit, said plainly), and a lease that asks for a sound deadening layer under a hard floor. Say why each adds time or a stage; no figure.

cards.title: What the houses were built with
cards.brief: Lime plaster and timber floors in the older terraces mean more preparation before a tile goes on; plasterboard in the newer homes decides what it can carry (the profile for the era; the Table A and E rows for what it means). Said as what the work meets, never as the state of the homes. No figure.

cards.title: Old floors that need a test before they come up
cards.brief: In older homes an old floor covering, and the dark adhesive under it, can be the kind that is tested before it is lifted (the Table C and E asbestos rows); if the test is positive the removal follows the safe method, which adds time and cost. Said plainly and never casually; no year or figure. From the profile where it gives the housing era.

cards.title: Patios on exposed ground
cards.brief: Outdoor tiling on an exposed site waits for weather clear of frost, needs a base and falls that shed water, and a tile declared for outside (the Table A and E outdoor rows). From the profile where it gives the exposure; only where the client has an outdoor page. No figure.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How much is coming off
cards.brief: The area of wall or floor, one room or several, a splashback against a whole bathroom, floor tiles on a thick bed against wall tiles. Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: How they were fixed and what they're on
cards.brief: Tiles on plaster that comes away with them and has to be made good, on cement board that stays and is used again, on a screed or on boards, floor tiles on a thick old bed (the Table A stages: inspect the substrate; the Table B signs row: the background breaks away with the tiles; the Table F row: a difficult substrate or thick bedding). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: Grinding the old adhesive back
cards.brief: The ridges of adhesive left when the tiles come off, ground back or made safe so the next finish sits flat, with the dust kept down by extraction or water as the job needs (the Table A stages: remove or make safe the residual bedding; the Table E cutting dust row; the Table F row: dust control). Never "dust free" (Table G).

cards.title: An old floor covering and the waste
cards.brief: Old floor tiles or a black adhesive under them checked before anything disturbs them, because the result changes the method (the Table A stages: check the age, the substrate and potential asbestos; the Table E row on asbestos beneath old finishes), said as a check, never an age or a date; the rubble bagged, carried out and taken away by a registered carrier (Table C waste duty of care). The waste taken away only from confirmed practices (waste_removal). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How much joint there is to do
cards.brief: The length of joint: one shower corner against every wall in the room, a floor against a splashback, small tiles with far more joint in the same area (the Table F row for this service). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: The state of the tiles round the joints
cards.brief: Tiles sound and well stuck, so the joints can be raked out without them moving, against tiles loose or cracked that come into the job; grout stained through, so it comes out rather than being coloured over, which only suits grout that is still sound (the Table A materials cell; the Table F row: localised repair with clean, sound tiles and a dry substrate). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

cards.title: What's under the old grout
cards.brief: A joint raked out to its full depth so the new grout has something to hold, never a skim over the old (the Table B done badly row: new grout fails if loose material is left behind); a leak behind the tiles or a floor that moves, which regrouting will not fix and which the job finds first (the Table A stages: inspect the joints and identify leaks or movement; the Table F row: substrate or leak repair); the silicone joints at the bath, the corners and the floor redone with it, never filled rigid (the Table E corners row). Say why each adds a stage.

cards.title: The grout and the corners
cards.brief: An ordinary cement grout against a resin one, a colour matched to what is there, mosaics with far more joint to fill, a reach into a tight shower corner, the silicone renewed with it (the Table A materials cell; the Table F row: reaction resin grout or renewed seals, hard to access corners). Never a grout class or a standard's number. A named product only from [CV: materials_methods]. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.
